title: Make cartoon videos for YouTube (no editing skills)
questionPatterns: make videos without showing my face
how do i make animated videos

steps.title: Write the script
steps.tool: Any free chat assistant (GLM, ChatGPT, Claude)
steps.how: Ask for a 60-second script in scenes with narration + visual descriptions. Then ask it to punch up the jokes twice.

steps.title: Generate the voice
steps.how: Paste narration, generate voiceover, download the audio. Try 2–3 voices on one line before committing.

steps.title: Generate consistent character images
steps.tool: Any image generator with reference images
steps.how: Design ONE character image, reuse it as the reference for every scene — consistency is what makes it feel like a show, not a slideshow.

steps.title: Assemble the video
steps.how: Drop images + voiceover on the timeline, add auto-captions, one background music track at low volume, export 1080p.

steps.title: Thumbnail + publish
steps.how: Generate 3 thumbnail options with big readable text, pick one, upload with your script's opening line as the description.

mistakes: Regenerating the character for every scene — inconsistent characters scream 'AI slop'. Reuse the seed/reference image.
Planning 10 videos before publishing 1. Make video 1, publish, learn, then batch.
Signing up for 5 paid tools before you have 1 video. Every step above has a free option.

title: Build your first chatbot
questionPatterns: how to use an api as a beginner
make a chatbot for my notes

steps.title: Understand what you're building
steps.how: Read 'What is an API (really)?' — 15 minutes that make the rest obvious.

steps.title: Get a free API key
steps.how: Create an account, generate a key, save it in a .env file — never in your code.

steps.title: Make your first raw API call
steps.how: Follow the 'Your first API call' guide — one command, real reply, every error explained.

steps.title: Wrap it in a loop
steps.how: Add conversation history to the script so it remembers context — that's the whole difference between 'a call' and 'a chatbot'.

mistakes: Starting with a fancy UI instead of terminal text. Get it working ugly first; pretty later.
Pasting the API key into the script itself. Use .env from day one.
Building for 'everyone' instead of yourself. Your own use case is the best first user.

title: Run AI on your own laptop (free + private)

steps.title: Check what your machine can run
steps.how: Match your RAM to model sizes: 8GB → 1–3B models, 16GB → 7–8B, 32GB → 13–14B.

steps.title: Install Ollama
steps.how: Download from ollama.com — it installs like any normal app, no terminal heroics needed for setup.

steps.title: Run your first local model
steps.how: ollama run llama3.2:3b — wait for the download, then chat. No key, no account, no internet after download.

steps.title: Level up the interface
steps.how: If you want a ChatGPT-style face over Ollama, install Open WebUI — or skip it; the terminal works.

mistakes: Trying a model too big for your RAM — it crawls or crashes. Check the size first, always.
Expecting frontier quality locally. Local models are impressive for their size, not magic.
Downloading models from random sites. Use Ollama's library or Hugging Face with high downloads.

title: Summarize your notes, PDFs and homework with AI

steps.title: Start manual: paste into a chat
steps.how: Paste your notes and ask: 'summarize in 5 bullets, then make 10 flashcards Q&A'. Learn what works before automating.

steps.title: Find the repeating pattern
steps.how: Notice which prompt format works for YOUR material — the reusable prompt is the automation waiting to happen.

steps.title: Automate it when it repeats
steps.how: Build it as: upload/paste → AI step with your proven prompt → output to a doc. Trigger by hand first, schedule later.

steps.title: Level up: ask questions about YOUR documents
steps.how: When summaries aren't enough, you want RAG — AI that answers from your actual files. That's the next path.

mistakes: Automating before knowing what prompt works — the AI step is easy; the prompt is the product.
Uploading private study material to random 'free PDF summarizer' sites. Use tools you trust.
Summarizing as a substitute for reading. Summaries are a map, not the territory.

title: Make thumbnails and images for your content
questionPatterns: how to make images with ai

steps.title: Pick one image tool and stick with it
steps.how: Free tiers exist everywhere. Pick one, learn its quirks deeply — switching tools every day teaches you nothing.

steps.title: Learn the anatomy of a good prompt
steps.how: Formula: subject + style + setting + mood + composition. 'A husky in a tiny lab coat, cartoon style, cluttered mad-science lab, excited mood, centered composition'.

steps.title: Design for the thumbnail's real job
steps.how: Thumbnails must be readable at stamp size: 1 subject, max 3 words of text, high contrast. Generate, then shrink to 10% and check.

steps.title: Keep a prompt library
steps.how: Save every prompt that worked, with the image. Your library becomes your style — consistency beats randomness.

mistakes: Judge image quality on the first generation — generate 4–8 options, pick, and refine the winner.
Text in AI images is often mangled; add text in an editor (CapCut/Canva), not the generator.
Chasing 'the best tool' instead of mastering the one in front of you.

title: Build your first website with AI (and deploy it free)
totalCost: $0 to start (~$12/yr for your own domain, optional)

steps.title: Decide the one job of the site
steps.how: One sentence: 'this site exists so that ___ can ___'. A site with one job beats a cluttered one every time.

steps.title: Generate content + structure
steps.how: Ask for: 5 sections, headline + one-line pitch per section, plain HTML/CSS single file. Reject the first version; ask for 'shorter, more human, more specific'.

steps.title: Open it and edit for real
steps.how: Open the HTML file, change real words, colors, and links yourself — reading real code is the fastest dev lesson there is.

steps.title: Put it online, free
steps.tool: Netlify Drop / GitHub Pages / Cloudflare Pages
steps.how: Drag the folder onto Netlify Drop — live URL in 30 seconds, no account gymnastics. Or push to a GitHub repo and enable Pages.

steps.title: Optional: your own name
steps.how: Buy a domain only after the site exists. Point it at your host. Do this last, not first.

mistakes: Spending a weekend on the logo and zero minutes on the words. Text does the convincing.
Buying a domain before a single page exists. Free hosting first, name later.
Trying to learn a framework before shipping a single HTML file. Ship ugly first.

title: Learn to code with AI as your tutor
totalTime: Ongoing — first tiny project in a week

steps.title: Pick one language and one reason
steps.how: Python for automating/analyzing, JavaScript for websites. 'Both eventually, one now.' Pick based on what you want to BUILD.

steps.title: Set the tutor loop
steps.how: Prompt: 'You are my coding tutor. Explain like I know nothing. After each concept, give me a tiny exercise and wait for my answer. Correct me, then continue.'

steps.title: Build the dumbest useful thing
steps.how: A calculator, a grocery list, a coin flipper. Tiny and YOURS beats big and tutorial-shaped.

steps.title: Make the AI read code TO you
steps.how: Paste working code from repos (Repo Radar) and ask 'explain every line like I'm new'. Reading real code is the secret curriculum.

steps.title: Start your track record
steps.how: Push every tiny project to a public repo. In 3 months your GitHub IS your resume.

mistakes: Letting the AI write everything while you nod. Type the code yourself — fingers are part of memory.
Course-hopping. One language, one project, two weeks — then reassess.
Building another to-do app when something in YOUR life annoys you daily. Personal problems are the best teachers.

title: Start a podcast or voiceover channel with AI

steps.title: Pick a narrow topic you can talk about for 50 episodes
steps.how: Ask for '20 podcast episode ideas about X for beginners'. If fewer than 10 excite you, narrow X further.

steps.title: Write episode 1 as a conversation script
steps.how: Two hosts beat one monologue. Ask for a script with natural interruptions and one moment of genuine surprise.

steps.title: Generate the voices
steps.tool: Any TTS tool with multiple voices
steps.how: Two distinct voices, consistent across episodes. Generate 3 test lines per voice before committing to a cast.

steps.title: Edit lightly and export
steps.how: Cut long silences, add intro/outro music (free libraries: Pixabay, YouTube Audio Library). Export MP3.

steps.title: Publish free
steps.tool: Spotify for Creators (or any free host)
steps.how: Upload, get an RSS feed, submit to Spotify automatically. You now have a podcast. Tell people.

mistakes: Perfecting the voice while the script is boring. Content first, voice second.
Buying a professional mic for an AI-voiced podcast. You don't need one — that's the point.
Publishing one episode and waiting for fame. Podcasts compound — plan 10 before judging.

title: Make short videos (Reels, Shorts, TikTok) with AI

steps.title: Write a 30-second hook script
steps.how: Ask for: 3-second hook, 20 seconds of value, 7-second payoff/CTA. Reject anything that doesn't grab in line one.

steps.title: Generate or gather visuals
steps.how: Mix: AI images for the unusual, free stock (Pexels) for the ordinary. B-roll exists to support words, not replace them.

steps.title: Assemble in CapCut
steps.how: Vertical 9:16 project. Auto-captions ON (most shorts are watched muted). One cut every 2–4 seconds.

steps.title: Post at a repeatable cadence
steps.how: 1 short/day for 14 days minimum before judging anything. Algorithms reward presence, not perfection.

mistakes: Making one 'perfect' short instead of 14 average ones. Volume teaches you what your audience wants.
Ignoring captions — a muted-watchable short doubles its audience.
AI-generating every frame. A mix of real/stock/AI reads as content; pure AI slideshows read as spam.

title: Study for any exam with AI (the honest way)
totalTime: Set up in 1 hour, then daily

steps.title: Turn the syllabus into a battle plan
steps.how: Paste your syllabus: 'make a day-by-day study plan, hardest topics first, with a review day each week'.

steps.title: Make flashcards, not summaries
steps.how: Ask for 15 Q&A cards per topic. Question on one side, answer on the other. Testing beats re-reading — this is the single biggest study-science finding.

steps.title: Run the quiz loop
steps.how: 'Quiz me on topic X, one question at a time. If I'm wrong, explain, wait, then ask again differently.'

steps.title: Teach it back (the Feynman move)
steps.how: 'I'll explain the topic; you find the gaps and holes in my explanation.' Being wrong out loud is studying.

steps.title: Sleep, spacing, repeat
steps.how: Same topic twice, days apart, beats cramming twice in one night. AI can schedule it; only you can sleep.

mistakes: Letting AI summarize instead of quiz you. Recognition feels like knowing; recall IS knowing.
Trusting AI's facts blindly for exams — it can be confidently wrong. Verify against your actual course material.
Studying for 5 hours once instead of 1 hour × 5 days.

title: Write better with AI (without it sounding like AI)

steps.title: Outline with AI, draft yourself
steps.how: Ask for 5 section headings and the one idea per section. Close the chat. Write the ugly first draft in your own words.

steps.title: Critique pass, not rewrite pass
steps.how: 'Critique this draft: what's unclear, what's padding, what's missing? Do NOT rewrite it.' Then you fix it — voice stays yours.

steps.title: Line-edit the lazy phrases
steps.how: Ask: 'flag clichés, corporate words, and sentences longer than 25 words.' Shorter words, truer sentences.

steps.title: Read it out loud before publishing
steps.how: The human edit AI can't do. If you stumble reading it, the reader stumbles too.

mistakes: Copy-pasting AI drafts. Readers smell it, and you learn nothing — the skill is in the editing.
Asking AI to 'make it engaging'. That's how you get confetti words. Ask it to make it CLEAR.
Publishing without reading aloud. Your ear catches what your eye forgives.

title: Research any topic with AI (verified, not hallucinated)

steps.title: Break the topic into 5 questions
steps.how: 'Break [topic] into the 5 questions a beginner must answer to understand it.' You now have a map instead of vibes.

steps.title: Ask with sources demanded
steps.how: Use a chat that can search the web, and demand: 'cite sources for every claim. If unsure, say unsure.' Treat every fact as a suspect until sourced.

steps.title: Verify the 3 claims that matter most
steps.how: Open the links. If a claim survives you reading the source, it's yours now. If not, you just avoided repeating a hallucination.

steps.title: Synthesize in your own words
steps.how: Write a half-page summary from memory, then check it against your notes. The gap list = what you didn't understand yet.

mistakes: Trusting fluent prose. Confidence is a writing style, not evidence.
Skipping the verification step 'just this once'. This is the whole skill.
Reading only one source's framing. Ask a second model to argue the opposite side.

title: Build a tiny game with AI (and play it tonight)

steps.title: Scope it to one mechanic
steps.how: One verb: run/jump/catch/click. Snake, not Skyrim. 'Catch the falling squares' is a real game and is finishable tonight.

steps.title: Generate a single-file HTML game
steps.how: 'Write a complete single-file HTML+JS game: [mechanic]. Canvas-based, arrow keys, score display, game over + restart.' Save as game.html.

steps.title: Play it, then change one thing
steps.how: Open the file. Then iterate: 'make the player faster', 'add a 30-second timer'. Each change teaches you one real concept.

steps.title: Make it yours
steps.how: Change colors, add a title screen, rename things. A game with your jokes in it is 10× more satisfying to show people.

steps.title: Ship it to friends
steps.how: Drag-drop the file → URL → send it. 'I made this' is the sentence that starts everything.

mistakes: Starting with your dream MMO. Finish 5 tiny games first — tiny games teach finishing.
Asking for big changes when stuck. Ask 'why is this broken?' and read the explanation.
Never showing anyone. Shipped-and-shared beats perfect-and-hidden.

title: Plan a month of social content in one sitting
questionPatterns: never run out of post ideas

steps.title: Pick one platform and one audience
steps.how: 'Beginners who want X' beats 'everyone'. One platform, 30 days. Expand later or die trying.

steps.title: Generate 30 ideas, keep 15
steps.how: '30 post ideas about X for [audience], mixed formats: tips, myths, mistakes, hot takes, mini-guides.' Kill the boring half yourself.

steps.title: Draft in batches by mood
steps.how: Draft all tips in one sitting, all myths in another. Same-mood batching beats task-switching.

steps.title: Schedule or post manually — but on time
steps.how: Tools matter less than rhythm. Pick a posting time and defend it like a meeting.

steps.title: Review weekly, double down
steps.how: Check which 3 posts moved. More of those, fewer of the others. AI helps create; data helps you decide.

mistakes: Being on 4 platforms at once. One platform done well beats four abandoned.
Letting AI write captions with zero editing — audiences taste it instantly.
Quitting at day 9. Organic reach compounds around week 4–6, not day 3.

title: Build a portfolio that gets you replies
totalTime: A weekend to build, ongoing to maintain

steps.title: Inventory what you've actually made
steps.how: Every project, script, automation, video, site — including the dumb ones. Proof of shipping is the currency; polish is optional.

steps.title: Pick 3 projects, write them as stories
steps.how: For each: problem → what you built → what broke → what you learned. Employers hire the learning, not the demo.

steps.title: Tailor the resume per application
steps.how: Paste the job post + your resume: 'reorder and rephrase my experience to match THIS role. Never invent anything.' Honesty is a feature.

steps.title: Make your GitHub page say something
steps.how: Pin the 3 projects, write one honest sentence about each. A profile with 3 explained projects > 30 mystery repos.

steps.title: Apply in loops of 10
steps.how: 10 applications, track replies, refine ONE thing, next 10. The portfolio compounds while you send.

mistakes: Listing skills, showing nothing. A 12-line script that runs beats a skills list of 20 words.
One generic resume for every job. Matching the job post (honestly) doubles callbacks.
Waiting for the portfolio to be 'ready'. Version 1 embarrassing, version 3 employed.

title: Design AI-made products (stickers, shirts, prints)

steps.title: Find one niche, not 'everyone'
steps.how: Browse bestsellers in a niche you actually understand (a game, a hobby, a profession). Inside knowledge = designs outsiders can't see.

steps.title: Build a consistent style with prompts
steps.how: One style formula, many designs: same art style + same palette + different subject. Series sell; one-offs don't.

steps.title: Check licenses and platform rules
steps.how: Read your image tool's commercial terms AND the marketplace rules (some restrict AI). Selling banned stuff = deleted shop, wasted weeks.

steps.title: Clean up and upload
steps.how: Upscale, remove backgrounds, exact sizes per product. Presentation quality is half the sale.

steps.title: Expect slow, then adjust
steps.how: Print-on-demand pays slowly. 20 designs minimum before judging; then make more of what moves.

mistakes: Using trademarked characters. Instant takedowns, possible strikes. Original niches win anyway.
Uploading raw generations without cleaning — buyers zoom in. Present professionally.
10 designs then quitting. It's a shelf game: more (good) products = more surface area for buyers.

title: Take your content global with AI translation

steps.title: Pick one language at a time
steps.how: Where do your current views/visitors come from? Pick the biggest non-native group. One language done well beats five done thin.

steps.title: Translate meaning, not words
steps.how: Prompt: 'Translate this into X. Keep the casual tone. Localize idioms and examples — if a joke doesn't translate, replace it with one that lands.'

steps.title: Have a native speaker sanity-check page 1
steps.how: One 10-minute read by a native speaker catches the embarrassing stuff AI misses. Then reuse their corrections as prompt rules.

steps.title: Publish separately, link both
steps.how: Separate URL/video per language, cross-linked. SEO and algorithms both prefer dedicated pages.

mistakes: Machine-translating idioms word by word. 'It's raining cats and dogs' becomes weather advice about animals.
Assuming English UI + translated body = done. Buttons and titles need love too.
Five languages on day 1. Do language #2 completely first, learn the cost, then expand.

title: Get dramatically better AI answers (prompting that works)
totalTime: Practice forever, good at it in a week

steps.title: Give the AI a role and a reader
steps.how: 'You are a [role]. Explain to a [specific reader] who knows [X] but not [Y].' Aimed answers beat generic ones instantly.

steps.title: Add context like a briefing
steps.how: What you tried, what happened, what 'good' looks like. 'It doesn't work' is not context; screenshots and error text are.

steps.title: Specify the output format
steps.how: 'Answer as: 1) verdict in one line, 2) why in 3 bullets, 3) what I should do next.' Format is half the usefulness.

steps.title: Iterate instead of restarting
steps.how: 'Closer, but shorter and skip the history.' Conversation beats regeneration — the model learns what you want.

steps.title: Keep a personal prompt library
steps.how: Save your proven patterns. Six months later, the library IS your skill — and it's personal, uncopyable by anyone else.

mistakes: One vague prompt then giving up. Bad answers are usually briefing failures.
Asking for 'the best'. Compared to what, for whom, on what budget? Specificity is everything.
Never asking AI to critique your prompt: 'what info do you wish I had given you?'

title: Make music with AI (background tracks to full songs)

steps.title: Decide: instrumental or vocal
steps.how: Instrumental for background (easier, safer to license). Vocals for actual songs (harder, more fun).

steps.title: Prompt like a music producer
steps.how: Genre + mood + instruments + tempo + use: 'chill lo-fi beat, nostalgic, soft piano, 75 bpm, background for study videos'.

steps.title: Check the license before using
steps.how: AI music tools differ wildly: some allow commercial use, some don't. Read before your video with 1M views has to come down.

steps.title: Mix at the right volume
steps.how: Music sits UNDER voice: roughly -20dB below speech. If you can't hear every word, the mix is wrong.

mistakes: Full blast music under voiceover. Mute test: if you notice the music more than the words, it's too loud.
Skipping license checks because 'it's AI'. AI-generated can still be license-restricted.
One generation and done. Generate 4–6, pick the one with the least weird artifacts.

title: Chat with your own documents (notes, PDFs, textbooks)

steps.title: Start embarrassingly simple: paste it
steps.how: One document, one question. If it fits in the context window, pasting IS the technique — no setup needed.

steps.title: For many docs: use a document-chat tool
steps.how: Upload files, ask questions, get answers citing YOUR pages. Cited answers are the feature to look for.

steps.title: For private docs: go local
steps.how: Sensitive stuff (contracts, medical, work docs) shouldn't go to random services. Local models keep data on your machine.

steps.title: Build the habit, not the system
steps.how: 'What did I decide about X?' works only if the docs go in as they happen. Input beats tooling.

mistakes: Building the perfect 'second brain' before asking a single question. Tool later, questions now.
Uploading sensitive documents to unvetted 'free PDF chat' sites. Privacy policy first, upload second.
Expecting magic on messy notes. AI answers from your docs inherit your chaos — clean input, clean answers.

title: Edit videos with the right tools (2026 picks)
questionPatterns: which video editor should i use

steps.title: Pick the editor that matches your goal (all verified this month)
steps.how: Phone clips / captions / TikTok → CapCut (free, easiest). YouTube talking-heads → CapCut or Descript (edit by transcript). Films, color, 'make it look expensive' → DaVinci Resolve (free). No install allowed → VEED in the browser. Forever-free and open source → Kdenlive.

steps.title: Do the rough cut first — story before sparkle
steps.how: Trim dead air and mistakes in timeline order. Don't touch effects yet; a tight cut beats a shiny mess every time.

steps.title: Auto-captions (the highest-ROI 60 seconds in editing)
steps.how: All three generate captions from speech in one click. 80% of social video is watched muted — captions are not optional.

steps.title: Turn one video into five shorts
steps.how: Paste the long video link; the AI finds the best moments, reframes vertical and adds captions. Post the top 2 by virality score.

steps.title: Export with platform presets
steps.how: YouTube: 1080p (or 4K if your machine is fine), H.264. Reels/TikTok/Shorts: 1080×1920 vertical. Don't touch bitrate settings at the start — presets exist for a reason.

mistakes: Paying $23/mo for Premiere in week one. Every editor above has a free path — earn the subscription with published videos.
Color grading before the rough cut. Fix the story, then make it pretty.
Ignoring captions. Muted autoplay is how most people will see your video.
Editing on a machine that can't handle it. If playback stutters in Resolve, drop playback resolution to 1/2 in settings.
